headline_marked: [[Qwenputer: A functioning, deterministic RISC-V CPU inside Qwen3.5]]
headline: Qwenputer: A functioning, deterministic RISC-V CPU inside Qwen3.5
summary: Qwenputer is an experimental Qwen 3.5 model with a RISC-V CPU embedded in its weights, using the model's Gated DeltaNet layers as RAM. This CPU runs within forward passes, executing C and MicroPython code without external tools.
details: Qwenputer is an experimental model built on a stock Qwen 3.5 4B, featuring a RISC-V CPU compiled directly into its weights. This CPU uniquely utilizes the model's own Gated DeltaNet (GDN) attention layers to function as its RAM. It can perform arithmetic operations and run C and MicroPython code entirely within the model's forward passes, requiring no external runtime or tools.

This is not a plugin, a tool, or a sandbox; the CPU is deeply integrated within the model's architecture. The project also incorporates an experimental in-model file storage system. The underlying mechanism leverages the specific properties of GDN layers.

Qwen3-Next and Qwen 3.5 models use Gated DeltaNet as their attention mechanism in three out of four attention layers. Each GDN head maintains a state matrix, and a delta rule continuously updates this state, effectively acting as a form of memory.

The key innovation involves modifying the GDN layers by setting the gate and write strength to 1, and using one-hot key encoding. This configuration allows every write operation to overwrite exactly one row and every one-hot query to retrieve an exact value, making the GDN layers function as precise, addressable RAM. This method is significantly more cost-effective than using normal attention for memory, as a GDN head's state size remains constant regardless of conversation length.

The concept of the delta rule acting as memory isn't new, but Qwenputer's approach makes it exact and addressable within a production model, reliably enough to run a full CPU. This modification unlocks the potential for compiling complex functionalities directly into model weights.

The CPU is compiled into the model weights without any training; a compiler directly sets every weight. It translates the CPU's circuit description into a series of small steps, which are then implemented as transformer layers: attention heads for lookups, feed-forward units for arithmetic, and DeltaNet heads for RAM.

The CPU executes as the model decodes, with each instruction generating a few tokens that trace its operation. These tokens include an address for memory writes, a value, and a step token to conclude the instruction, making the CPU's execution visible within the model's output.

The embedded CPU is a 32-bit RISC-V core (RV32IM, plus Zba extension and a bignum unit). It occupies 11 layers within Qwen's 32 layers. This CPU has successfully passed official riscv-tests, its programs match qemu outputs, and it has run 18 million instructions free-running without a single error.
The Qwenputer model and its code are publicly available on Hugging Face, ModelScope, and GitHub, allowing developers to explore and build upon this novel integration of a CPU within an LLM.

Further research built on Qwenputer explores how hybrid models can conceal their reasoning in RNN states to evade CoT monitoring, and how compiled weights can serve as untamperable inbuilt monitoring tools for the model itself.

headline_marked: [[GitLab instance targeted by critical CVE-2026-97229 exploit]] after patch release
headline: GitLab instance targeted by critical CVE-2026-97229 exploit after patch release
summary: An attacker attempted to exploit a critical GitLab vulnerability on an Alpine Linux instance, coming close to success. Though no evidence of compromise was found, the instance was rebuilt from scratch as a precaution.
details: On October 20 and 21, an attacker tried to exploit a critical GitLab vulnerability (CVE-2026-97229) on an Alpine Linux instance. This occurred a week after the fix was released for the bug, which has a CVSS score of 10.0 and affects GitLab's CI configuration due to an underlying flaw in Ruby's Onigmo regular expression engine.

The attack crashed GitLab worker processes eight times. In four of those crashes, the attacker got partway through the exploit, suggesting they were tuning it to the exact build by downloading the GitLab container image. While no evidence of code execution was found, it could not be ruled out, leading to the decision to rebuild the instance from scratch.

The Alpine Linux GitLab instance was still running version 19.3.4, which did not include the October 12 fix. The fix was a patch to Ruby bundled by GitLab, but Alpine's image used standard Ruby, which did not receive the patch until October 27.

Users running GitLab with their own Ruby (from source or custom container images) must upgrade Ruby to versions 3.3.13, 3.4.12, or 4.0.9 or later. Those using the `alpinelinux/gitlab` container image should pull `alpinelinux/gitlab:19.3.6` again, as the image published on October 27 contains the fixed Ruby.

All passwords for `gitlab.alpinelinux.org` accounts have been reset as a precaution. Users will need to set a new password via the "Forgot your password?" option upon the instance's reopening. Users are also advised to change any reused passwords on other sites due to observed automated login attempts against Alpine's GitLab.

Checks confirmed that the `aports` repository, packages, and October 21 releases were not tampered with. These checks were performed against records the attacker could not reach, including developer clones and builder records, and are being extended to cover the period until the instance was closed on October 27.

The underlying bug in Ruby's regular expression engine means any program compiling regular expressions from untrusted input is exposed, not only GitLab. Alpine Linux versions 3.21, 3.22, 3.23, 3.24, and edge now ship with fixed Ruby versions; users should run `apk upgrade` to apply the update.
